newsitem.title: FINLAND: Bruton expects EU budget stability pact at Dublin.
newsitem.headline: Bruton expects EU budget stability pact at Dublin.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said on Friday he expected the European Union summit next month in Dublin to agree on a budget stability pact for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
"I would expect that we will reach the agreement in Dublin," Bruton told a joint news conference here with Finnish Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen.
An agreement on the budget stability pact could also be reached later without derailing monetary union, Bruton said.
"If we don't reach it in Dublin, that's not the end of the day. It can be reached in January or February," he said.
"There is time to finalise the stability pact even after Dublin," Bruton said.
"But from the point of view of all concerned, to maintain the pace, the momentum, it is desirable that we should reach an agreement in Dublin, he added.

Ireland, which holds the rotating presidency of the European Union until the end of this year when it hands over to the Netherlands, will arrange a summit of EU heads of state and government in Dublin on December 13-14.
But doubts have also been raised that a stability pact to ensure budgetary discipline among eventual EMU member states might not be reached at the summit.
Earlier this week, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said it would be better to wait for a good result on the proposed stability pact than to move too quickly and have an unfavourable result.

Asked what allowances would be made in the stability pact for flexibility to deal with economic downswings, Bruton said the degree of flexibility was still under negotiation, but that flexibility would be needed.
"Clearly we do need to have an arrangement that is viable politically and economically to take account of genuinely exceptional circumstances that affect a particular economy," Bruton said.
But Bruton said there was concern, felt strongly by Germany, that exceptional circumstances should not become a form of routine flexibility that would be used for political reasons.

"They want to ensure that exceptions are genuine, based on genuinely verifiable and short-term economic circumstances, that there is not any general loosening of discipline resulting from these arrangements," Bruton said.
He added there was concern that monetary union should be based on disciplined economic policies in the countries that join it.

"There is a general and genuine concern that (the proposed common European currency) the Euro should be solidly based on economic policies that are transparent and real and involve real discipline," Bruton said.

In addition to the stability pact, Bruton said the Dublin summit would work to finalise the legal framework for EMU, to confirm the arrangements for relations between countries that join the Euro in the first phase and those remaining outside, and to confirm the January 1, 1999 start date of EMU.
